audit.story: Round one analysed 20 shortlisted engineers and picked Gilbert09, webjunkie, pauldambra, Piccirello and haacked. An independent audit then re-checked every input against the raw PR data and found that the shortlist had missed strong engineers (eli-r-ph and MattBro were added), a quality rate whose numerator and denominator used different PR sets, self-repair that the follow-up-fix metric could not see, and explanations that claimed more than the merged PRs show. We fixed the quality calculation, added self-repair and human versus AI-only approval counts, rewrote the claims to match what merged, and had two independent decisions, head-to-head comparisons and a devil's-advocate pass re-rank all 22 candidates. The top three held; rafaeelaudibert entered at 4th, haacked stayed 5th after beating Piccirello head-to-head in both presentation orders, and Piccirello fell to 6th.

top5.positioning: The de facto owner and highest-throughput engineer of PostHog's warehouse-sources product: he keeps the ingestion pipeline running through a constant stream of incident and data-correctness fixes, expands the source catalogue at industrial scale, and in October began moving every integration credential behind a new credentials service.

delivery.rationale: He is first of 20 by a wide margin, and the lead survives once volume is stripped out. Counting only episodes that contain a major PR, he has 130 against 20 for the runner-up on delivery. The major work also lands in the categories the rubric weights most: incidents (#110610), data correctness (#113196), billing (#114623, #87465) and security (#81559, #82905, #123893, #125154). I discounted the templated catalogue PRs heavily, and that discount is the only reason this is not a 10.

system.rationale: He built several reusable abstractions that other teams now depend on: destinations, typed source cursors, the integrations SDK with a ratchet, and the credentials service with kill switch and watch-based propagation. Other authors build on his files at the 97th percentile. I stop at 8, not 9, because most of the platform work landed in the last three weeks of the window, so adoption beyond his own migrations is not yet visible, and peers asked for changes on the SDK PR (#124844, webjunkie).

quality.rationale: Peer-behaviour numbers are good for this volume: no reverts, 99% first-pass approval, quality rate 0.98 (6th of 20). The absolute counts still need weighing. Peers made follow-up fixes to 31 of his PRs, 9 of them major. One of his own design choices appears to have caused a fleet-wide outage: #86546 refused a half-configured client, and two months later #122385 restored the environment fallback after a two-hour worker outage. Peers also pushed back on a batch of nine templated sources on 2026-08-05, and his deep reads score Q=1 on several platform PRs (#124844, #86986, #108390, #122385). A 7 is solid but not exemplary.

team.rationale: He is a broad, reliable approver with real reach (52 authors, 23 teams), and the few review comments that have text are substantive. The pattern is still approval-heavy: 269 approvals against 1 changes-requested. Only 7 people explicitly asked for his review, and his reviewer importance flow is negligible. His team value comes mostly from unblocking others, such as customer-success engineers shipping sources and peers building on his code, not from catching problems in review. That matches his percentiles of about 63–76 on the team columns.

core_contributions.title: Keeping the warehouse sync pipeline correct and alive
core_contributions.what: A long run of major-tier fixes to the shared ingestion path. He rewrote the V3 batch-claim query so its gates run once per group or run instead of per candidate batch, which ended an incident that stalled every loader pod (#110610). He made append syncs roll back unfinished runs, which stopped duplicate rows (#113196). He stopped orphaned Running jobs from being billed (#114623), added autovacuum settings to the new partitions to prevent claim slowdowns (#111096), and added a stalled-schedule gauge plus a repair command for syncs that silently stalled for days (#102914). Earlier he fixed Redshift OOMs, a sync that had failed for 46 days (#79500), and the repartitioning budget and resume logic (#80079, #95747).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Every customer warehouse source shares this pipeline. These bugs meant the whole fleet stalled, rows were duplicated (a data-correctness problem), or customers were billed for jobs that never ran.
core_contributions.outcome: The two incident fixes are the highest-scored deep reads in his pack (16 pts, V3 C3), and nothing he shipped was reverted. 129 of his 211 major-tier PRs are fixes, most of them on this path.

core_contributions.title: Credentials service and integrations SDK
core_contributions.what: He built a platform that moves integration secrets out of pod environment variables. Steps: an integration-service deployable (#79462); Kubernetes watch-based secret distribution, so replicas pick up a rotation within about 1s (#116078); OAuth client keys for every integration read from the service with a kill switch (#120995); an integrations SDK with three auth types and a semgrep ratchet against direct model access (#124844). He then migrated call sites in 21 products (#125029), the PostHog/EE code (#125005), Tasks (#124994) and the Slack app (#125018).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: This is security work across the company: credential rotation and revocation, plus keeping warehouse credentials out of code paths that should not see them. It touches integrations owned by many teams.
core_contributions.outcome: The SDK and the service are live, and the call-site migration finished inside the window. On-demand deep reads score #124844 at 7.29 pts with L=3 and #120995 at 5.92 pts. The rollout did cause one fleet-wide credential-read outage, fixed by #122385 (see red_flags).

core_contributions.title: New warehouse capabilities: destinations, cursors, incremental views, catalogue breadth
core_contributions.what: He added a multi-destination abstraction so a source can sync its tables to external Postgres (#86986, 12.13 pts), then wrote destination writers for BigQuery, Databricks and S3 (#87964, #87963, #87965). Alongside this he shipped catalogue growth at scale: dozens of new sources per month, with the changelog crediting him for '54 new Data Warehouse sources' and 'Hundreds more warehouse source tables'.
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Destinations make the warehouse a two-way product, and cursors are the foundation for new source types such as Kafka. The breadth of the catalogue is what customers see first.
core_contributions.outcome: 412 of his PRs are cited in the public changelog, the most of the 20 candidates. Most of the catalogue PRs are templated (about 870 add-source or add-table PRs), so this work counts for breadth, not depth.

insights.insight: His output runs at a pace that implies a heavily tool-assisted workflow: about 33 merged PRs a day on average and about 52 a day in the peak week, and review replies signed 'via talyn.dev'. The AI-share metric therefore understates AI use for him, and his catalogue volume should be read as a well-run generation pipeline, with his judgment showing in the incident and platform PRs.

He is the single point of ownership for warehouse sources: 88% of his PRs are in the area and he leads 64 authors there. Three warehouse peers review almost all of his PRs. That is efficient, but the area's correctness depends heavily on one author's judgment and a small reviewer set.

He works far outside his home area when the problem calls for it: the Tasks sandbox backend (hogland routing, billing attribution, OOM fixes), MCP security fixes and the desktop and mobile inbox. He covers 56 areas in total.

Gilbert09.counter_evidence: Several things argue against the top-tier reading. (1) Volume: about 32% of his PRs are templated source, table or GA additions, and his 1.14M changed lines are dominated by them. Delivery points over-credit this, and I discounted it. (2) His PR descriptions frame credentials-service fixes such as #122385 as improvements. The behavioural evidence shows the outage came from his own earlier design (#86546), so I scored that against quality. (3) Peers requested changes on 17 PRs, including a batch of nine templated sources on 2026-08-05 and the integrations SDK (#124844, webjunkie). (4) Only 19 of 2939 PRs (0.6%) were deep-read in the stratified sample, plus 6 on demand, and 32% of the diffs were truncated. The quality of the routine and substantive bulk is inferred from triage summaries, not verified. (5) As a reviewer he almost never blocks (1 changes-requested out of 284 reviews), so team credit rests on reach, not on correction. None of this overturns delivery or system, but it is why overall confidence is medium, not high.

pauldambra.positioning: A very high-throughput platform engineer (652 merged PRs in 13 weeks) who owns PostHog's shared frontend platform and spends most of his time on cross-cutting performance, security and reliability work that every product team and every user sits on.

role.how_they_create_impact: He removes cost from paths everyone uses: the app boot and bundle path (HTML 544KB to 10KB, ~1.5 MiB of eager JS removed per scene), the Django request path (one fewer query per session request, N+1 batching across 275 team-scoped models), and the CI and test infrastructure. Alongside that he ships a steady stream of access-control and data-integrity fixes and smaller product features (SQL box plots, DORA health tab, dashboard tabs). He then locks the gains in with CI ratchets and guards so they do not regress.
role.network_summary: Trusted author with a wide downstream footprint rather than a heavy reviewer. His approval-graph trust rank is 3rd of 20 and 100 distinct authors later built on files he changed. 12 people requested his review and he approved 38 authors across 15 teams, so he is a go-to reviewer for frontend-platform and developer-experience work. But almost all of his network importance comes from authoring, and he gave only 1 changes-requested review in the window. He sits in community 1 with bridge rank 5, a moderate bridge between product teams and platform. His own PRs pass first review 98% of the time, slightly below the 20-person median of 0.99.

core_contributions.title: Frontend boot and bundle performance campaign
core_contributions.what: A sustained campaign on the shared frontend shell: moved the ~474 KB inline esbuild chunk map into a content-hashed static file (#94059), per-chunk minification for byte-stable deploys (#122919), lazy-loaded query node renderers per scene (#127333), split app-context loading into boot and full stages (#128226), scene prefetching during boot (#127407), and dozens of PRs pulling alerts, cohorts, Max/AI, billing and zod off the eager path. Gains are locked in by a CI check that fails new upward frontend layer imports (#126768).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: This is the code path every logged-in and logged-out PostHog user runs on every page load. #94059 cites Asian users (27% of traffic) paying 3.3s p75 first paint for the inline map; shrinking the boot document from 544 KB to 10 KB and removing 1.1-1.6 MiB of eager JS per scene is user-visible latency across all products.
core_contributions.outcome: 192 PRs in workstream 1 (5 major, 122 substantive, 654 points), 124 PRs across workstreams whose title or summary targets bundle/boot cost, 83 of them since 2026-10-12. Deep reads: #94059 9.8 pts, #122919 5.5 pts, #127333 5.53 pts (on-demand). One dormant flagged experiment (#119225) was rolled back by himself (#119292) after it slowed scene rendering.

core_contributions.title: Django request-path, ORM and auth hardening
core_contributions.what: Backend platform work on the Django layer: team-scoped querysets default to a peer-batching fetch mode so lazy relation reads cost 2 queries instead of N+1 across 275 models (#126463), a PostHog auth middleware that loads the session user with its organization in one query (#126421), a test-time guard against lazy loads plus fixes (#126622), a per-route Postgres query-count metric (#126313), deterministic pagination tiebreakers (#104980), an incident fix for OAuth refresh-token reuse detection that had caused 300s+ endpoint latency (#83929), and a data-integrity fix for settings PATCH wiping server-managed integration tokens with row locking (#108163).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These change default behaviour for every API request and every team-scoped model, so the blast radius is repo-wide. #83929 resolved a production incident, #108163 prevents silent loss of Slack/Teams/GitHub integration state, and the N+1 work comes with a production metric so others can verify the gains.
core_contributions.outcome: 48 PRs in workstream 3 (5 major, 25 substantive, 180.9 points). Deep reads: #108163 16 pts (C3 L3), #83929 13 pts (C3), #126463 9.62 pts (C3 L3, Q1), #104980 5.9 pts. #126463 and #126421 merged in the last week of the window, so peer follow-up on them is not yet observable.

core_contributions.what: A run of security fixes outside his home area: project-access check before Signals Slack notifications (#102477), livestream membership recheck that closes streams when access is revoked (#108135), binding hobby Temporal ports to localhost (#114015), OAuth scope-version check that background token calls could bypass (#94116), Cloud egress block for external TypeSafe requests (#108333), and hardening shared LemonTable/project tree menus against unsafe link schemes (#127334).

That is why later authors of the same files (100) and approval-network centrality sit in the top 3 while major episodes sits at p34.

Security and data-integrity fixes are an under-counted second line of value: six major access-control or exposure fixes, several only a few lines long (#114015 is 4 lines, C3), done outside his home area.
Output accelerated sharply in the last three weeks (109 PRs in the week of 2026-10-26) while his review volume fell, so the end of the window is his least-reviewed and least-matured work.

custom_analyses.question: Is the frontend performance work a sustained, deliberate campaign, and how large are its individual pieces?
custom_analyses.why: Over a third of his PRs are in workstream 1 and the late-window weeks are his busiest, so the question is whether this is one strategic programme or a pile of small lazy-load PRs inflating volume.
custom_analyses.finding: It is a sustained programme that accelerates: 124 PRs across workstreams target bundle or boot cost, rising from 27 in September to 67 in October and 30 in November up to the window end on 2026-11-03; his two busiest weeks are 2026-10-12 (87 PRs) and 2026-10-26 (109 PRs). workstream 1 alone has 100 PRs since 2026-10-12 (2 major, 67 substantive). The anchor PR #94059 is genuinely large (9.8 pts), but the on-demand deep reads of later pieces score modestly: #127333 5.53 pts (Q1) and #119225 5.53 pts, and #119225 was reverted by himself in #119292. role.how_they_create_impact: He closes security holes in PostHog's identity surface (OAuth revocation, ID-JAG token exchange, CIMD, MCP prompts, secret API tokens) and builds the plumbing that lets AI agents use PostHog safely: scope step-up challenges, WebMCP, the MCP tool catalog and the hog CLI. core_contributions.title: OAuth, ID-JAG and API-token security hardening
core_contributions.what: A sustained series of fixes across PostHog's OAuth server and token handling: client authentication and binding on the ID-JAG jwt-bearer grant (#113013), identity linking by IdP subject instead of email (#113014), jti replay protection and lifetime caps (#113012), gating CIMD partner promotion on the client's own opt-in (#83980), blocking the CGNAT range in the shared SSRF validator (#86093), stopping cross-client token revocation (#105396), race-safe connected-app revocation (#84974) and hiding the project secret API token from callers lacking its scopes (#127775).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Each of these is an account-takeover, privilege-escalation, auth-bypass or data-exposure path on a surface every customer and every third-party MCP/OAuth client touches. Security is in the highest criticality class of the rubric.
core_contributions.outcome: 13 of his 26 major PRs are auth/security fixes. Deep reads score them 7.8 pts to 16.0 with C=3 on most (#113013, #86093, #113014, #127775, #84974). No reverts in the workstream; one (#84974) needed a follow-up fix.

core_contributions.title: Making the PostHog MCP server safe and usable for AI agents

core_contributions.why_it_matters: #105547 closed a cross-customer data leak (13 pts, the highest-scored deep read in his sample). The step-up and catalog work turns MCP from an ad hoc integration into a scoped, reusable platform that other surfaces (hog CLI, WebMCP, wizard) consume.

Piccirello.positioning: PostHog's hands-on application-security engineer: he finds and closes privilege-escalation, SSRF and credential-leak holes across the whole product and ran the multi-week program that took the app's Content Security Policy from report-only to enforced.

role.how_they_create_impact: Mostly through his own small-to-medium security fixes that land across many teams' code (auth, permissions, warehouse sources, CDP, replay, CI), plus reusable guardrails (a single access-precedence resolver, a shared connect-time host check, semgrep rules, Renovate pins, agent security guidance) that keep the same class of bug from coming back. Reviewing is a second, narrower channel: few but deep security findings on other teams' PRs.
role.network_summary: Trusted, frictionless author but a narrow approval base: every one of his 105 reviewed PRs passed first time with zero change requests, and 84 other authors later built on files he changed. His approvals come mainly from his own team (feliperalmeida reviewed 40 of 105 PRs), so his PageRank-style trust is low. As a reviewer he is a cross-team security approver rather than a hub people route work through.

core_contributions.title: Closing authorization and credential holes in the Django platform
core_contributions.what: A steady stream of auth and permission fixes: one precedence resolver for project access so API checks, User.teams and all_users_with_access agree (#114423); a single access-checked function for minting personal API keys (#114412); scoped-key privilege escalation into project secret keys (#105467); invite privilege escalation (#122926); passkey sessions for deactivated users (#113790); public self-service leaked-key revocation and its follow-up hardening (#81587, #81631).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These are cross-tenant and privilege-escalation classes of bug in the core permission layer every product team depends on; #114423 removes the drift that let digests and notifications email users about projects the API denies them.
core_contributions.outcome: 19 major and 33 substantive PRs in the workstream; the on-demand deep read scored #114423 at 16 pts (V3 C3 N2 L3), the highest possible band, and #105467 and #122926 at 7.8 pts. No reverts.

core_contributions.title: Content Security Policy rollout: measure, repair, enforce, tighten
core_contributions.what: A planned program of about 55 CSP-related PRs from early September to mid October: report-only shadow policies to measure what would break (#104099, #113389), flags and seams to enforce safely (#98025, #106400), a run of fixes so features kept working under enforcement (#99457, #100642, #101381, #104022), then tightening wildcard hosts to named hosts (#106238) and enforcing on shared and embedded documents (#116719).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: An enforced, narrow script-src/connect-src is what turns an injected script from a full account takeover into a blocked request; #106238 closed the path where injected code could load from an attacker-controlled PostHog project.
core_contributions.outcome: Policy enforced on signed-in, login, shared and embedded pages by 2026-10-15, wildcard hosts replaced by named hosts, and a shadow-policy pipeline for the next tightening step. The cost was roughly 24 repair or relaxation PRs while enforcement exposed broken features.

core_contributions.title: SSRF and DNS-rebinding defences for warehouse sources
core_contributions.what: Pinned every direct Postgres connection to the addresses already validated by the host policy (#95376), turned the connect-time check into a shared helper and extended it to Temporal.io with a registry-wide test over every host-taking source (#101362), re-validated hosts at connect time (#93742), and closed a cross-tenant S3 read path at the model layer (#81598).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Warehouse syncs dial customer-supplied hosts from inside PostHog's network; a host that resolves public on check and private on connect reached internal addresses. The shared helper makes the fix apply to future sources by default.
core_contributions.outcome: Both sampled PRs scored 9.6 pts (V2 C3 N2 L2), the top of his stratified sample, though each also carried review findings (Q=1, '1 must fix').

insights.insight: He is a high-criticality, low-volume-per-PR contributor; a volume-weighted delivery score (15th of 20) understates him, while major-episode count (2nd of 20) and deep reads of his top PRs (16 pts, 13, 9.6) are a better read.
His fixes tend to become guards that run without him: shared helpers with registry-wide tests, one access resolver, semgrep rules, Renovate pins and agent security guidance for the review bot.
His work spans many teams' code (warehouse sources, CDP, replay, surveys, MCP, feature flags), but almost all of it is authored by him rather than routed through others' reviews.

custom_analyses.question: Is the CSP work a coherent platform program, and how much of it is repair work caused by his own enforcement?
custom_analyses.why: CSP is his single largest theme, and a long run of 'fix(csp): allow X' PRs could mean either careful incremental hardening or a rollout that kept breaking product features.
custom_analyses.finding: About 55 of his 144 PRs mention CSP (31 substantive, 4 major). Classifying their titles by keyword (approximate): about 11 add measurement or reporting, about 16 tighten or enforce, and about 24 relax the policy or repair a feature enforcement broke. The phases run in order: report-only shadow policies and an embed seam (09-03 to 09-10), a burst of repairs once enforcement started (09-11 to 09-24, 33 workstream 1 PRs in that span, peaking at 26 PRs in the week of 09-21), wildcard-to-named-host tightening (#106238, deep-read 7.8 pts, 09-24) and enforcement on shared and embedded documents (#116719, 10-15). It is a deliberate program with measurement first, but enforcement did reach users before all breakages were found (admin confirmation dialogs, HogQL editor, replay image export).
custom_analyses.effect: system stays 7 (a real program with reusable measurement, but a security primitive rather than a product platform); quality 8 to 7 because roughly 24 PRs went to repairing his own rollout.

custom_analyses.question: How did he handle the compromised eMudhra CA incident, and did the response create follow-on breakage?
custom_analyses.why: The late-October week is his second-largest by PR count and is dominated by dependency bumps; I wanted to know whether this is mechanical churn or company-level incident response.
custom_analyses.finding: Between 10-21 and 10-23 he shipped about 10 PRs that remove the compromised roots from every trust store PostHog ships or runs: Node in production images and CI (#121580), the Python image CA bundle (#121599), the customer-deployed metrics agent (#121626), the MCP server (#121776, then #122294), desktop builds (#121627, #122821), gRPC (#122221) and bundled Codex (#122820). He then added Renovate managers so Node pins auto-bump (#122387, #122319). The MCP server needed a CA-bundle stopgap and a second PR moving it to Node 24.22.1 with a pinned undici to avoid a crash-loop; the deep read scored that fix 16 pts (V3 C3 N2). The data does not show who introduced the crash-loop.
custom_analyses.effect: delivery held at 8 rather than 7: one person covering every runtime within 3 days, with automation against recurrence, is company-level critical work even though each PR is small.

custom_analyses.question: Where does his reviewing carry weight, and how independent is the approval he receives?
custom_analyses.why: team leverage is missing for him and approval-network centrality is low, so I needed the raw review mix to judge the team angle.
custom_analyses.finding: He gave 108 reviews on 98 PRs by 28 authors in 19 team buckets (developer-experience 29 PRs the most); 94 are approvals, 12 comments, 2 change requests. The non-approvals cluster on a few security-sensitive PRs (SAML/SCIM #78527 three times, sandboxed HTML artifacts #111376 four times, a release-workflow tag ruleset #106016 marked blocking), and every review comment listed in the dossier is marked as line changed afterwards. On the receiving side, feliperalmeida, his security-team colleague, reviewed 40 of his 105 reviewed PRs (38%) and the security team 40 overall, which explains a approval-network centrality of 0.0079 (17th) against webjunkie's 0.02 (1st). Compared with webjunkie, the Django-platform area leader, he has nearly as many major PRs (42 vs 47) on about a quarter of the volume (144 vs 559 PRs), but far less reviewer reach.
custom_analyses.effect: team stays 6: individual reviews are high-signal, but volume of substantive reviews and the approval graph do not support 7.

core_contributions.what: Built persons_dedup to remove duplicate (team_id, uuid) person rows so the missing unique index could be created (#81532), then hardened it for production with a survivor gate and reachability checks (#85945). Reworked person deletion to tombstone by default and bound hard deletes by version so revived persons are not hidden (#111380, #111670, #111396, #111239), and built a divergence scan, classifier and repair command with restore, merge, republish and fold verbs (#111675, #111676, #117440, #117445, #118360).

core_contributions.outcome: Merged: 40 PRs in workstream 1 (19 major, 16 substantive) over 81 days, plus the personhog RPCs in workstream 3 that the repair tools call. core_contributions.title: Capture rate limiter and v1 ingestion robustness
core_contributions.what: Rebuilt the capture global rate limiter's Redis behaviour: bounded per-tick work to enforceable keys (#83250), clamped and then spread key expiry (#89726, #106188), made it fail open on Redis read outages (#107014), stopped busy pods losing count updates (#116680) and added two-cluster sharding (#117238). In capture v1 he removed whole-batch drop paths: a timestamp char-boundary panic (#103274), an out-of-range offset panic (#116599), strict option parsing (#108097), duplicate-uuid batch rejection (#122305), and capped lz64 decompression against resource exhaustion (#102546).

core_contributions.title: Scheduled ClickHouse deletion sweep and Postgres cleanup drain

core_contributions.why_it_matters: GDPR and project deletions only complete when these background jobs actually run; before #94573 the cohort sweep crashed on memory exhaustion, and an unbounded tombstone backlog grows without the drain.
core_contributions.outcome: Merged: 19 PRs in workstream 4 (2 major, 11 substantive) over 38 days; #94573 deep-read at 9.62 pts. The drain needed ordering and version-bound fixes two weeks after it was scheduled (#111239, #111396), which he also shipped.

mayteio.positioning: The highest-volume builder on the Workflows/Messaging product, who in October drove the migration of PostHog's own transactional email (password resets, invites, alerts) off Customer.io onto Workflows, while also hardening the CDP job queue and realtime cohorts that every workflow depends on.

role.how_they_create_impact: Ships a steady stream of end-to-end product work in Workflows and Messaging (174 + 38 PRs) and repeatedly reaches down into the shared CDP/Node pipeline and Rust cohorts to fix the reliability and correctness bugs his product exposes: a queue-stalling counter overflow, OOM crashes on cohort recomputes, unbounded tenant templates, zero-member realtime cohorts. Reviews heavily for his two closest teammates and approves work for authors across 23 teams.
role.network_summary: Core member of a tight three-person Workflows loop: dmarchuk and meikelmosby review 83 and 74 of his PRs, and he reviews 60 and 80 of theirs. Beyond that loop he is a broadly trusted approver, signing off PRs from 43 authors across 23 teams with approval-network centrality 6/20. He is rarely sought out explicitly as a reviewer, though: only 4 people requested his review. His own PRs almost never need correction in review, but 7 were followed up by fixes and 1 was reverted after merge. 88 other authors later built on files he changed, above the median of 77.

core_contributions.title: Moving PostHog's own transactional email off Customer.io onto Workflows
core_contributions.what: Built the full path for transactional email as real workflows: an `api` trigger type and versioned one-step email workflows (#117663), a send endpoint and cross-SDK contract (#123556), per-template sender/reply-to (#121871), flag-gated per-recipient routing with idempotency-keyed retries (#122019), mapping of all 35 internal templates (#122502), sensitive-data redaction (#120520), delivery-status tracking in ClickHouse (#124696), and fixes for duplicate sends after a Valkey outage (#123481) and silently dropped password resets (#123492).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These emails carry sign-up verification, password resets and invites for every PostHog user, so failures are account-access incidents; the migration also removes a third-party dependency and turns Workflows into a transactional email product that customers can use.
core_contributions.outcome: Flag-gated rollout infrastructure is in place with region-split flags (#123060) and a real kill switch (#125322); 55 PRs mention transactional email or Customer.io, 51 of them merged in October. Full cutover is not visible in the window.

core_contributions.title: Reliability of the CDP/Workflows execution pipeline
core_contributions.what: Fixed failure modes in the shared Node CDP pipeline that runs every workflow and destination: saturating cyclotron job counters at all 13 increment sites so one row cannot stall a queue (#97591), batching cohort-trigger lookups to stop consumer OOM crashes (#118407), bounding tenant Liquid rendering with parse, time and memory limits (#94119), and treating transient DNS errors as retriable (#108193).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: The cyclotron bug held up workflow email sending for over a day; the Liquid issue let one tenant's template stall or OOM shared workers. These are multi-tenant availability fixes, not feature polish.
core_contributions.outcome: Two of his three highest deep-read scores (13 pts for #97591, 9.6 on-demand for #94119) come from this work; no follow-up fixes or reverts are recorded against these PRs.

core_contributions.title: Data correctness in realtime cohorts that gate flags and workflows
core_contributions.what: Fixed realtime composed cohorts being certified ready with zero members (#121092, Rust), preserved the origin of cascaded membership changes so backfills do not re-trigger workflows (#118434), locked cohort criteria edits on cohorts used by active workflows after an incident (#118447), and added realtime cohort-membership workflow triggers (#116951).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: A zero-member cohort makes feature flags, workflows and triggers silently match nobody, which is a cross-product data-correctness failure that users cannot detect.
core_contributions.outcome: #121092 received the highest on-demand deep-read score of any of his PRs (16 pts, V3 C3 N2).

insights.insight: He works top to bottom: product features in Workflows and Messaging, then follows the failures his product exposes down into shared Node CDP and Rust cohort code that other teams also depend on.

His and dmarchuk's output is almost mirror images: similar PR counts (290 vs 265) and delivery (702 vs 616), but he has more major PRs (38 vs 26) and wider review reach (23 vs 9 teams) at the cost of a lower quality rate (0.95 vs 0.99).
AI co-authorship is low (8 PRs, 3% share) with no AI-assisted PR reverted or fixed, so his volume is not explained by agent-generated PRs.

core_contributions.title: Keeping long-running cloud task runs alive and lossless
core_contributions.what: Built and then hardened sandbox rotation before TTL (#86676), the activity guard that stops rotation from discarding live worktrees (#109870), checkpointing that preserves pending user messages and no longer deletes workspace files (#116932), the turn-success flag that records wall-clock-capped runs that delivered a PR as completed (#108247), fail-closed Redis log-append locks (#83195, #99208), and GitHub-verified clone denials so transient token errors stop killing runs (#123981).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These are the failure modes of a paid product: runs dying at sandbox expiry, lost uncommitted work, lost logs and mis-recorded outcomes. #108247 notes that over 90% of implementation runs that opened a PR ended in the mis-recorded state.
core_contributions.outcome: 209 PRs in the workstream, 16 major; the deep-read PRs here are among his highest scored (#109870 16 pts, #108247 13 pts, #116932 13 pts, #86676 12.1 pts). Rotation needed several follow-up fixes before it was stable (see custom analyses).

core_contributions.title: LLM gateway routing, billing and spend control for cloud runs
core_contributions.what: Fixed streamed token usage and provider labels so Kimi/GLM generations bill real token counts (#94154), added the 70%/85% budget guard that steers runs to commit and open a PR before the gateway cuts them off (#102980) and its retry fix (#115263), opt-in per-user spend caps (#109055), and a series of model-routing fixes where requested models silently fell back to Opus or failed (#116194, #120877, #122180, #106614).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Billing correctness and spend caps directly affect revenue and customer trust; silent model fallbacks charged users for a different model than they chose.
core_contributions.outcome: 23 PRs in the gateway workstream (4 major) plus the budget guard in Desktop; #115263 deep-read 5.9 pts with all quotes verified.

core_contributions.title: Security boundaries for cloud agent sandboxes
core_contributions.what: Treated cloud checkouts as untrusted so repo-defined extensions, settings and MCP servers cannot load in cloud Pi sessions (#120934), rejected symlink escapes in the desktop clone tool (#90123), enforced Modal egress allowlists for restricted VMs (#79608), enforced model entitlement server-side on every run path (#80331), and closed the Gmail duplicate-mailbox signup gap (#108223, #107552).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Agents running untrusted repository code with user credentials is the main security risk of the product; these PRs close credential-exfiltration and abuse paths.
core_contributions.outcome: Five major security-class PRs in the window; #120934 deep-read with C=3 (critical) and 7.8 pts, and #108223/#107552 are among his 2 changelog entries.

insights.insight: His work reads as an on-call owner of a young, paid product: most majors are fixes to outage, data-loss, billing or security failure modes of cloud agent runs, shipped in small increments at about 23 PRs per active week.
Reviewers almost never push back on him (2 change requests in 272 reviewed PRs), so peer review is not where his defects get caught; they show up as follow-up fixes after merge, mostly his own.
Output dipped to 4 PRs in the week of 2026-09-07 and 10 in the week of 2026-10-05, then recovered; there is no release-driven spike, the throughput is steady across 15 active weeks.

custom_analyses.question: Are his unsampled major PRs as strong as the sampled ones, or is the major tier inflated by self-described urgency?
custom_analyses.why: Only 7 of 26 major PRs were in the stratified deep-read sample, and fix PRs often describe themselves as critical. The on-demand budget lets me check the most consequential-looking unsampled ones.
custom_analyses.finding: The six on-demand deep reads scored 7.82 pts, 5.92, 16.00, 9.19, 7.29, 13.00 (mean 9.87), above the sampled major stratum mean of 8.5; all quotes verified. Three scored C=3 (critical): #120934 (cloud checkouts treated as untrusted to block credential-reading extensions), #109870 (rotation discarding active worktrees, the highest P in his pack at 16.0) and #116932 (checkpointing that cleared pending messages and deleted live workspace files). #81235 (peer messaging, 3005 lines) is the clearest new capability. The weakest was #90123 (5.92 pts), whose summary notes a remaining must-fix around in-root symlinks.
custom_analyses.effect: delivery 7 → 8 because the unsampled majors are real data-loss and security fixes, not inflated labels; the #90123 must-fix is carried into red_flags.

commands: IMPACT_OUT=out_full .venv/bin/python -m impact.fine.query tatoalo prs --area "Product: Tasks" --since 2026-10-01 --tier major

custom_analyses.question: How does his team footprint compare with peers in his orbit who rank higher on leverage or reach?

core_contributions.title: Buffered Postgres CDC made safe: ordering, deletes, resets and slot hygiene
core_contributions.what: He built the pre-write CDC load-resolution layer (ordering guard, keep-highest dedupe, delete-enrichment verification, fail-closed flag) that unblocked buffered S3 ingress, then added buffered ingress itself, forced the v3 pipeline for buffered schemas, routed CDC snapshots through the buffer, and closed a long list of failure modes: reset races that wiped tables, truncates silently ignored, primary-key changes leaving stale rows, quiet runs letting WAL build up until the slot dropped, expired buffer files and ETag-based buffer deletion to stop double-counted billable rows.
core_contributions.why_it_matters: CDC is the path customers use for live Postgres replication into the warehouse. Each bug class here produced wrong data with no error (lost deletes, duplicated or stale rows), customer database WAL growth, or billing for rows that were never new.
core_contributions.outcome: 43 PRs mention CDC or replication slots (23 major), peaking in September (24). core_contributions.what: He fixed data that customers were losing or being charged for without knowing: Stripe webhook upserts overwriting complete invoice rows with partial payloads, Stripe basil API breakage and tie-breaking that left paid invoices open, Help Scout syncs missing conversation statuses, Postgres replica re-reads duplicating and dropping rows, xmin wraparound dropping rows, resumable syncs duplicating rows after worker rotations, a lost-update race that resurrected soft-deleted table links, and repartition rewrites that OOM-killed workers forever (an incident affecting 16 customers).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Revenue analytics reads these Stripe tables directly, and a warehouse that silently duplicates or drops rows breaks every downstream join, insight and billing count without anyone seeing an error.

core_contributions.what: A run of security fixes: escaping column names in the ClickHouse s3()/deltaLake() structure argument (expression injection), validating Google token_uri against Google's endpoints for BigQuery and then generalising the check across every Google Cloud key-file integration and export, pinning validated addresses against DNS rebinding for Redshift/MySQL/PlanetScale/Postgres, MySQL and database TLS certificate verification, and per-view edit checks closing an authorization bypass in data modeling.
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Warehouse sources accept customer-supplied hosts, key files and column names; each of these was a path to SSRF, credential exfiltration or query injection against PostHog infrastructure.

workstreams_summary.title: 杂项（含 3 条实质及以上）

thmsobrmlr.positioning: Product-analytics engineer who spent the window retiring PostHog's legacy insight Filter system end to end, while shipping a steady stream of fixes for insights that silently returned wrong numbers.

role.how_they_create_impact: Runs long, staged migrations in the insights stack: moves editors and readers off the lossy legacy filter shape onto query nodes, then deletes the old converter, endpoints and Filter classes. Along the way he finds and fixes data-correctness bugs (dropped series fields, wrong retention and funnel results, stale all-time ranges) and isolates product code behind facades. 222 PRs, 23 tiered major, zero reverts.
role.network_summary: Reliable approver inside product-analytics rather than a sought-after reviewer: he approved 34 authors across 17 teams, concentrated on sampennington (24 PRs) and MattPua (13), but only 4 people explicitly requested his review. His code is a foundation others build on: 89 distinct authors later changed files he touched. He rarely needs correction: first-pass approval 0.98 and only 2 follow-up fixes against 222 PRs. He is not a bridge between communities, and almost all importance flowing to him comes from authorship, not reviewing.

core_contributions.title: Retiring the legacy insight Filter system
core_contributions.what: A staged migration across about 46 PRs from 2026-08-27 to 2026-11-03: stopped converting legacy filters on read (#96074), removed the legacy trend and funnel endpoints (#97647), deleted the filters-to-query converter (#100835, 9,060 lines), deleted the 40-mixin legacy Filter (#104270), moved the insight, experiment and settings series editors onto node-native pickers (#115882, #115906, #115946), switched chart labels, tables, drill-downs and CSV export to read the query series, and finally deleted EntityFilter, ActionFilter and the filters package (#127312, #127983).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: The legacy round-trip silently dropped query fields the editor did not show (math_multiplier, revenue currency, fixedProperties, warehouse source type), so any UI edit could change an insight's numbers; it also affected experiment metric configs and customer-analytics settings. Removing the dual representation eliminates that class of bug for every team that embeds the series picker (experiments, CDP, replay, heatmaps).
core_contributions.outcome: About 49k changed lines across the program, the legacy converter and Filter classes gone, and no reverts. #115882 is one of his two highest-scored PRs (13 pts); #96074 kept filters-only insights from 500-ing the insights list (5.92 pts).

core_contributions.title: HogQL query-engine correctness and safety
core_contributions.what: Fixes and guards in the query engine behind insights: bounded the trends/stickiness per-series fan-out to 200 queries with 10-way concurrency (#102774), fixed stale cached all-time start dates on warehouse saved views (#127976) and all-time insights on String timestamp columns that skipped older rows (#127979), made missing cohorts return 400 instead of 500 (#99500), and added system.event_definitions / property_definitions tables (#124827).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These are silent-wrong-result and resource-exhaustion bugs: a single insight could exhaust worker threads and the shared Postgres pool, and saved-view insights could drop rows for up to 24 hours without any error.
core_contributions.outcome: 24 PRs, 6 tiered major; deep reads score #102774 at 7.82 pts, #124827 at 7.5 pts and #127976 at 5.92 pts.

core_contributions.title: Cross-product data and security fixes
core_contributions.what: Fixed CSV uploads that were introspected with RFC 4180 quoting but read with quoting off, leaving tables unqueryable (#104005); closed two prompt-injection gaps in PostHog AI context handling (#103158, #103615); fixed AI observability renderers hijacking the global person column across core tables (#103997).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Data warehouse uploads that save but fail every query, and forged trusted-context tags in the AI agent, are correctness and security issues outside his home area that he picked up and fixed.
core_contributions.outcome: #104005 scored 13 pts (tied highest), #103997 7.8 pts; both PostHog AI hardening PRs tiered major.

insights.insight: His highest-impact work is invisible to per-PR counting: the deletions and reader switches that retire the legacy filter model are tiered routine one by one, but together they remove a class of silent data-loss bugs for every product that embeds the series picker.
AI-assisted output at high volume without a quality cost: 149 of 222 PRs (0.67, 4th of 19) are AI co-authored, yet only 1 of them was reverted or follow-up fixed.
He is a builder first and a reviewer second: 98% of the importance flowing to him in the network comes from authorship (749.7 of 763.05).

custom_analyses.question: Is the large number of routine-tier refactors actually one coherent platform migration, and how big is it?
custom_analyses.why: 68 routine and 19 mechanical PRs would normally dilute his profile, but many titles reference legacy filters, query nodes and series pickers, which suggests one program rather than unrelated chores.
custom_analyses.finding: About 46 of his PRs (49k changed lines, 4 major, 15 substantive, 25 routine) form one staged migration from 2026-08-27 to 2026-11-03: stop converting on read (#96074, 5.92 pts), delete the converter (#100835, 9,060 lines), delete the legacy Filter (#104270, 1.32 pts), move series editors to query nodes (#115882 13 pts, #115906, #115946), switch readers to the query series (#116839, #116861, #116862), and delete the remaining types (#127312, #127983). The busiest week (2026-10-12: 32 PRs, 5 major) is the node-native picker cutover. Pure deletions score low individually, but they are the steps that make the correctness fixes permanent.
custom_analyses.effect: system 7 → 8, because the routine tiers hide a multi-team platform consolidation that peers then built on (89 downstream authors).

custom_analyses.question: How much of his fix work addresses silent wrong results rather than cosmetic bugs?
custom_analyses.why: Delivery should weight data correctness heavily for an analytics product, and 71 of his PRs are fixes; the tier labels alone do not show whether they matter to users' numbers.

None of these was reverted.

Against sampennington he has far more major PRs (23 vs 4), a similar quality rate (0.98 vs 0.97) and more downstream authors (89 vs 83), but lower team leverage (472.89 vs 575.47), fewer review requesters (4 vs 9) and slower first reviews (24.85h vs 15.42h median).

On delivery, the matrix places him 13th of 20 and he has no changelog entries and no landmark PR; the case for grade 7 rests on the correctness value of his fixes and on reading the routine-tier migration as one program, which is my judgment rather than a peer behavior. workstreams_summary.title: 杂项（含 4 条实质及以上）

gantoine.positioning: Developer-experience platform engineer who spent the window running a sustained campaign to unclog PostHog's CI and Trunk merge queue for every team, while also hardening the security of the team's AI review and auto-approval bots; his reach is repo-wide but his measured delivery and downstream footprint sit near the bottom of the 20.

role.how_they_create_impact: Removes friction that every engineer pays on every PR: narrowing merge-queue lanes so unrelated PRs stop serializing, deflaking tests that kick batches out of the queue, moving redundant master suites to crons, and adding lint checks and tooling (hogli verify, workflow-plan, WF009) that keep CI correct. Secondary: security hardening of Stamphog/PostHog Review and webhook credentials.
role.network_summary: A high-volume, broad approver rather than a sought-after expert. He gave 415 reviews on 403 PRs for 71 authors across 27 teams, which drives team leverage to 3rd of 19. But 94% of those reviews are approvals (391), only 6 requested changes, and only 4 people explicitly requested his review. More than half of his reviewing (222 of 403 PRs) goes to two devex teammates, webjunkie and rnegron, and rnegron in turn reviews 93 of his 164 reviewed PRs: a tight devex review pair. Trust rank is at the median; bridge rank=2 in community 1 suggests he connects devex to many product teams through CI approvals. Others rarely build on his files, which is expected for CI/workflow files but means the system angle cannot lean on peer build-on behavior.

core_contributions.title: Merge-queue throughput and CI reliability program
core_contributions.what: Over 90 days he shipped 122 CI/tooling PRs (66 substantive, 2 major). The core thread is the Trunk merge queue: hand-narrowed lane rules early on (#78351, #79744, #81045, #90085, #89288), then lanes derived from code structure (#90078 Rust lanes from the affected-services determinator, #110140 import-derived nodejs sub-lanes, #117151 impacted targets from the GitHub compare API), then Trunk Dynamic CI in learning mode (#101929). Around it: deflaking tests that evicted queue batches, a WF009 lint check that derives MCP filter coverage from the import graph (#94179), quarantine gating (#90158), and moving master suites to hourly crons (#90195).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Merge-queue serialization and flaky kickouts tax every engineer in the monorepo; a lane that claims every target makes one team's PR block everyone else's.
core_contributions.outcome: Self-reported effects include claimed proto targets cut from 162 to roughly 2-104 (#81045), PRs no longer serializing behind 436 files (#90085), master matrix runs cut from about 160/day to at most 24/day (#90195) and about 1,300 runner hours saved on queue branches (#88762). These figures come from his PR descriptions; no reverts were recorded in the workstream, and Dynamic CI (#101929) is non-gating, so its savings are not yet realized.

core_contributions.title: Security hardening of Stamphog and PostHog Review
core_contributions.what: Made the Stamphog auto-approval worker re-run the engine gates itself against a pinned file list before posting an approval, escalating to a human when the sandbox verdict cannot be confirmed (#125439); fail-closed on symlinked trusted-file parents (#125413); pinned the sandbox Python interpreter (#121220). In PostHog Review he moved triggering to @posthog comments with a Stamphog handoff (#124327), added a round cap (#119856) and per-PR cost attribution (#117301).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Stamphog approves PRs automatically; if untrusted PR code can influence its verdict, it becomes a path to merge unreviewed code into the monorepo.
core_contributions.outcome: The on-demand deep read of #125439 scored 16 pts (V3 C3 N2), the highest single score in his pack; three workstream 6 PRs all close concrete trust-boundary gaps. Outside the stratified estimate, so not reflected in delivery.

core_contributions.title: Webhook credential secrecy and supply-chain trust fixes
core_contributions.what: Added a Secret headers input to the CDP webhook destination so credential headers are encrypted, never returned by the API and kept out of queue params and logs, while hardening template sync to fail loudly instead of deleting templates (#96545); added Standard Webhooks HMAC signing (#90307); separately refreshed CA bundles in llm-gateway and Streamlit images to stop trusting compromised eMudhra intermediates (#122682).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These are the few user-facing and security-critical items in his window: customer webhook tokens were previously stored and moved in plaintext.
core_contributions.outcome: #96545 is one of his 4 major-tier PRs with deep-read 13 pts; #122682 is major-tier (6.3 pts).

insights.insight: His impact is breadth of reach through shared CI rather than code others build on: later authors of the same files (18th) and importance flow (19th) are near the bottom, while teams approved is 1st, which fits a CI owner whose files are workflow configs.

The highest-scoring PR in his pack (#125439, 16 pts) merged on the last day of the window and was only found through an on-demand deep read; the stratified estimate rests on 15 sampled PRs and misses it.
Security work is a recurring secondary theme across three workstreams (Stamphog trust boundaries, webhook secrets, CA bundles), more than his devex label suggests.

MattBro.positioning: Growth-team engineer who owns the security and billing correctness of PostHog's partner integrations (Vercel Marketplace, Stripe app, partner provisioning, OAuth/CIMD) while also running the growth signup-enrichment and ICP-scoring pipeline, shipping a small number of high-criticality fixes rather than high volume.

role.how_they_create_impact: He finds and closes account-takeover, privilege-escalation and credential-spoofing paths in the flows partners use to create, link and bill PostHog accounts (Vercel SSO and connect, Stripe marketplace OAuth, partner provisioning, OAuth introspection and token cleanup), then adds the billing guardrails that keep partner-paid organizations from being charged twice. In parallel he maintains the growth enrichment pipeline (Harmonic, Clearbit, AI labeler, Hog-based ICP formulas) that scores new signups for sales.
role.network_summary: A focused pair-reviewer inside one growth sub-team, not a broad approver. He approved work for 11 authors across 4 teams, and 44 of the 64 PRs he reviewed belong to one teammate, rafaeelaudibert. His own PRs are reviewed by the same pair: rafaeelaudibert on 47 and fercgomes on 22 of 79 reviewed PRs. Even so, 13 people requested his review, so he is a recognized go-to reviewer for partner-auth and enrichment changes. He rarely needs correction. His approval-network centrality is mid-pack and he is not a bridge between communities. 54 other authors later changed files he touched. Almost all his importance flow comes from authoring, not reviewing.

core_contributions.title: Closing account-takeover and spoofing holes in partner auth and OAuth
core_contributions.what: A run of security fixes across the OAuth server and partner sign-in flows: client-credentials introspection scoped to the verified caller (#82258), CIMD verification tokens bound to their metadata URL (#74913) and partner-only promotion to confidential clients (#80748), the Stripe marketplace OAuth app split from the provisioning orchestrator so Stripe-account members can no longer mint deep-link sessions as the installing admin (#84698, #87261), symmetric and private keys rejected in client JWKS (#110193), a proxy-generated nonce for the OAuth-proxy callback (#97529, workstream 6), Vercel SSO requiring a PostHog login and then the mapped user's verified email before linking (#97534, #107067, workstream 4), browser-bound Vercel connect sessions and callback state (#106042, #116411), partners required to sign provisioning requests with private_key_jwt (#112182), and Stripe headless linking restricted to Stripe-verified emails (#119795).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: These are the flows through which partners create and log into PostHog accounts. delivery.rationale: Every authored PR is a substantive or major fix of a production failure or a broadly felt cost, and #80285 alone ended a fleet-wide customer-facing outage. But the volume is the lowest of the 20 candidates (delivery 63.02, p0; median 616.02), there are no landmark PRs, no changelog entries, and seven consecutive weeks (2026-09-07 to 2026-10-19) with no authored PR. High criticality per PR, thin overall: stable effective contribution, not a team pillar on delivery.

system.rationale: Shows real systems judgment (single-flight lease row instead of N pods redoing global sweeps; module-wide plus per-listener MPTCP opt-out) and the CI work improves shared tooling for every frontend PR. But no new abstraction or platform others built on: only 3 later authors touched his files (later authors of the same files p0) and the CI changes are too recent to show adoption.

quality.rationale: Clean peer record: 0 reverts, 0 follow-up fixes by others, 9/9 PRs approved with no changes requested, quality rate 1.0 (rank 1/20). Fixes ship with guarding tests (memory floor test, MPTCP regression tests) and the loader fix was verified on prod data. Held below 8 because the base is tiny (4 mature PRs) and two deep reads could not verify their quality quote (#95304 Q=0, #126537), so the risk-control evidence is partly self-reported.

team.rationale: He carries a large review load (928 reviews on 854 PRs, team leverage 2124.59, rank 2/19) and responds fast (0.18 h median), which keeps the most prolific author in the repo unblocked. But the load is narrow and mostly non-blocking: 91% of reviewed PRs are Gilbert09's, 10 change requests out of 928 reviews (9 of them in one morning on 2026-08-04), up to 71 approvals in a single day, only 4 people request his review and approval-network centrality is p0. The sampled comments are concrete (cache sentinel unpickling bug, resume-cursor skipping a day) and 80% of his suggested changes were adopted, so the gate is not empty; it is shallow per PR and confined to one stream.

grade.delivery.label: Delivery grade
grade.delivery.formula: L3 evaluator grade 1–10: user value, criticality (outage, data correctness, security, billing), novelty. 9–10 company-critical or benefits many teams · 7–8 core pillar of the team · 5–6 steady effective contribution · 3–4 local contribution · 1–2 marginal

grade.system.label: System grade
grade.system.formula: L3 evaluator grade 1–10: abstractions, platforms, tooling, performance; whether others build on his code. 9–10 company-critical or benefits many teams · 7–8 core pillar of the team · 5–6 steady effective contribution · 3–4 local contribution · 1–2 marginal

grade.quality.label: Quality grade
grade.quality.formula: L3 evaluator grade 1–10: reverts, fixes by others, change-request rounds, risk control. 9–10 company-critical or benefits many teams · 7–8 core pillar of the team · 5–6 steady effective contribution · 3–4 local contribution · 1–2 marginal

grade.team.label: Team grade
grade.team.formula: L3 evaluator grade 1–10: reviews that catch real problems, adopted suggestions, review requests, network position. 9–10 company-critical or benefits many teams · 7–8 core pillar of the team · 5–6 steady effective contribution · 3–4 local contribution · 1–2 marginal

grade.overall.label: Overall grade
grade.overall.formula: L3 evaluator overall grade 1–10 with confidence. 9–10 company-critical or benefits many teams · 7–8 core pillar of the team · 5–6 steady effective contribution · 3–4 local contribution · 1–2 marginal

R.label: Reference score R
R.formula: 0.50·delivery + 0.20·system + 0.15·quality + 0.15·team; each angle = mean of its quant / agent / behaviour percentiles among candidates (0–100); unknown signals left out

R_rank.label: Rank by R
R_rank.formula: position when candidates are sorted by R alone

borda.label: Borda points
borda.formula: sum over rankers of (11 − rank) for ranks 1–10; ties broken by pairwise wins

stability_freq.label: Weight robustness
stability_freq.formula: share of 1000 draws (each angle weight × U(0.5, 1.5), renormalized) in which he is top 5 by R; ≥70% stable, 40%–70% borderline, below = verdict only

gate.a.label: Gate (a): substance
gate.a.formula: ≥2 major-tier PRs or ≥1 landmark, or team leverage in the candidates' top 3

gate.b.label: Gate (b): no quality red flag
gate.b.formula: reverted < 3 times and follow-up-fix rate not in the candidates' worst 20%

gate.c.label: Gate (c): ranker agreement
gate.c.formula: at least 2/3 of rankers place him in their top 7

delivery_hat.label: Delivery estimate
delivery_hat.formula: Σ over contribution episodes of (max PR points + 0.25 × the rest); deep-read P replaces tier points on sampled PRs
delivery_hat.plain: importance-weighted points of shipped work (1–16 per PR, related PRs grouped)

changelog_weighted.label: Changelog entries (weighted)

changelog_weighted.plain: changelog mentions of his PRs, weighted by prominence

issue_reactions.label: Issue reactions
issue_reactions.formula: 👍 reactions on issues his PRs close
issue_reactions.plain: 👍 on the issues his PRs closed

core_share.label: Core-path share

core_share.plain: share of his work in core systems (query engine, ingestion, data layer)

deepread_L.label: Deep-read leverage
deepread_L.formula: mean LLM leverage score L (0–3) over his deep-read PRs
deepread_L.plain: leverage of his sampled PRs as judged by a model reading the diff

deepread_Q.label: Deep-read quality
deepread_Q.formula: mean LLM quality score Q (0–3) over his deep-read PRs
deepread_Q.plain: quality of his sampled PRs as judged by a model reading the diff

changes_requested_rounds.label: Change-request rounds
changes_requested_rounds.formula: mean CHANGES_REQUESTED reviews per PR of his (lower is better)
changes_requested_rounds.plain: change-request rounds per PR (lower is better)

review_leverage.label: Review leverage
review_leverage.formula: human reviews given × ln(1 + distinct authors served)
review_leverage.plain: reviews he gave, weighted by how many different authors he served

comment_line_changed_rate.label: Comments acted on

comment_line_changed_rate.plain: his review comments whose line was changed afterwards

downstream_authors.label: Later authors of the same files

quality_rate.label: Quality rate

quality_rate.plain: his substantial PRs never reverted or fixed by someone else

review_requesters.label: Review requesters

tier_points.label: Tier points

mass.label: Importance mass

team_score.label: Team score

episodes.label: Episodes

selected_by.label: Selected by

q.label: Quality rate

q.plain: his substantial PRs never reverted or fixed by someone else

people.label: Contributors

route.critical.label: Route: critical

final_n.label: Final

audit.label: Recall audit

review_coverage.label: Review-detail coverage
review_coverage.formula: review comments, threads and review requests were fetched for at most 60 PRs he authored and 80 PRs he reviewed (ranked by tier points, then recency) plus his deep-read sample; comment-based metrics use only those PRs

ai_only_approved.label: AI-only approvals
ai_only_approved.formula: window PRs whose APPROVED reviews all came from bot reviewers / all window PRs (and / human-authored PRs)

audit_round.label: Audit and correction
audit_round.formula: an independent audit re-checked every input against the raw PR data; fixes were applied and all candidates re-decided

decision_agreement.label: Decision agreement
decision_agreement.formula: two decision agents ranked the 20 independently (the second blind to the first); overlap of their top 5, Kendall τ over the full ranking, and pairwise re-checks asked in both presentation orders (consistent = same winner both times)

fetch_reconciliation.label: Fetch reconciliation
fetch_reconciliation.formula: for every day in the window, merged PRs fetched = GitHub search count for that day

quote_check.label: Quote verification
quote_check.formula: every evidence quote an LLM cites must be a verbatim substring of the PR title, body, diff or review text; a failed quote lowers that sub-score by 1

llm_cost.label: LLM cost

bot_prs.label: Bot PRs

m.team_leverage.formula: human reviews given × ln(1 + distinct authors served)
m.team_leverage.plain: reviews he gave, weighted by how many different authors he served

m.requested_by.label: Review requesters
m.requested_by.formula: distinct humans who requested his review
m.requested_by.plain: different people who asked him for a review

m.downstream_authors.label: Later authors of the same files
m.downstream_authors.formula: distinct authors who later built on files he changed (hub files excluded)
m.downstream_authors.plain: other engineers who later changed files he had changed

m.cross_team.label: Teams approved for

m.changelog_prs.label: Changelog PRs

m.changelog_prs.plain: his PRs cited in PostHog's public changelog

m.ai_share.label: AI co-authored share
m.ai_share.formula: his PRs whose commits are Co-authored-by an AI assistant (data/commit_authors.json) / his PRs
m.ai_share.plain: his PRs co-written with an AI assistant

m.self_driving_share.label: AI-agent PR share
m.self_driving_share.formula: AI-agent (self-driving) PRs credited to him / his PRs
m.self_driving_share.plain: his PRs opened by PostHog's AI agent on his behalf

m.first_pass_rate.label: First-pass rate
m.first_pass_rate.formula: his PRs approved with no changes requested / his reviewed PRs
m.first_pass_rate.plain: his reviewed PRs approved with no change request

m.changes_requested_rate.label: Changes-requested rate
m.changes_requested_rate.formula: his PRs that received CHANGES_REQUESTED / his reviewed PRs
m.changes_requested_rate.plain: his reviewed PRs that got a change request (lower is better)

m.trust_rank.label: Approval-network centrality
m.trust_rank.formula: PageRank on the approval graph (reviewer → author)
m.trust_rank.plain: approval-network centrality: PageRank of who approves whom

m.importance_flow.label: Importance flow
m.importance_flow.formula: PR points propagated over the person–PR graph to authors and substantive reviewers
m.importance_flow.plain: PR importance credited to him as author or substantive reviewer

n.first_pass_rate.label: First-pass rate
n.first_pass_rate.formula: his PRs with ≥1 approval: share with no change request before the first approval

n.changes_requested_rate.label: Changes-requested rate
n.changes_requested_rate.formula: his human-reviewed PRs: share that got ≥1 change request

n.changes_rounds_mean.label: Change rounds (mean)
n.changes_rounds_mean.formula: his PRs that got a change request: mean number of change-request reviews

n.changes_adopted_rate.label: Change-request resolution (proxy)
n.changes_adopted_rate.formula: (reviewer, PR) pairs where he requested changes: share where he later approved and the PR has ≥2 commits (proxy for the author pushing a fix)

n.approved_authors_n.label: Authors he approved
n.approved_authors_n.formula: distinct authors he approved; n = PRs he approved

n.teams_covered_n.label: Teams he approved for
n.teams_covered_n.formula: distinct teams (data/team_map.json) of the authors he approved; n = PRs he approved

n.requested_by_n.label: Requested as reviewer by
n.requested_by_n.formula: distinct people who requested his review; n = covered PRs he authored or reviewed

n.built_on_by_n.label: Later authors of the same files
n.built_on_by_n.formula: distinct authors who continued development on his code (continue events); n = his window PRs

n.fixes_given.label: Fixes for others
n.fixes_given.formula: follow-up fixes he made to others' PRs / others made to his; n = his window PRs

n.fixes_received.label: Fixed by others
n.fixes_received.formula: follow-up fixes he made to others' PRs / others made to his; n = his window PRs

n.reverts_given.label: Reverts of others
n.reverts_given.formula: reverts he made of others' PRs / others made of his; n = his window PRs

n.reverts_received.label: Reverted by others
n.reverts_received.formula: reverts he made of others' PRs / others made of his; n = his window PRs

n.trust_rank.label: Approval-network centrality
n.trust_rank.formula: weighted PageRank on the approval graph (reviewer → author, weight = approvals): an approval from someone who is himself approved by trusted people carries more

n.importance_flow.label: Importance flow
n.importance_flow.formula: each window PR's points (deep-read P, else triage tier points) flow 1.0 to its author and 0.3 to each substantive reviewer (changes requested or a written review)

g.communities.label: Communities
g.communities.formula: Louvain (seed 7) on the undirected review graph (approve + changes_requested + comment); purity = share of team-known members in the community's most common team; hub = most reviews inside

g.bridges.label: Bridges
g.bridges.formula: top 10 by betweenness on the review graph

g.single_points.label: Single points
g.single_points.formula: product area (main area of the PR by weighted lines) where one person gives ≥80% of ≥5 approvals

r.human_approved_prs.label: PRs approved by a human
r.human_approved_prs.formula: his merged PRs with at least one human APPROVED review

r.ai_only_approved_prs.label: PRs approved only by an AI bot
r.ai_only_approved_prs.formula: his merged PRs whose only approvals came from bot reviewers

r.no_approval_prs.label: PRs merged with no approval
r.no_approval_prs.formula: his merged PRs with no APPROVED review at all

r.human_approved_major_prs.label: Major PRs approved by a human
r.human_approved_major_prs.formula: his major/landmark PRs with at least one human approval

r.ai_only_approved_major_prs.label: Major PRs approved only by an AI bot
r.ai_only_approved_major_prs.formula: his major/landmark PRs whose only approvals came from bots

r.no_approval_major_prs.label: Major PRs merged with no approval
r.no_approval_major_prs.formula: his major/landmark PRs with no APPROVED review

r.self_repaired_prs.label: PRs he later repaired himself
r.self_repaired_prs.formula: his PRs that a later PR of his own explicitly fixed (invisible to the follow-up-fix metric, which counts only others)

f.merged_prs.label: Merged PRs in the 90 days
f.merged_prs.formula: his merged PRs in the window (bots and AI-agent PRs excluded)
f.merged_prs.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.major_prs.label: PRs rated major or landmark
f.major_prs.formula: his PRs that LLM triage rated major (8 pts) or landmark (16 pts)
f.major_prs.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.active_weeks.label: Weeks with a merged PR
f.active_weeks.formula: 7-day bins of the window (of 13) with at least one of his PRs merged
f.active_weeks.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.revert_rate.label: His PRs that were reverted
f.revert_rate.formula: reverted PRs / merged PRs; a revert must explicitly reference his PR (lower is better)
f.revert_rate.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.fixed_share.label: His PRs later fixed by someone else
f.fixed_share.formula: PRs fixed by another engineer within 14 days (explicit reference) / merged PRs (lower is better)
f.fixed_share.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.first_pass.label: First-pass approval
f.first_pass.formula: his reviewed PRs approved with no change request first
f.first_pass.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.reviews_given.label: Reviews given to other authors
f.reviews_given.formula: human reviews he gave on others' PRs, and the distinct authors they went to
f.reviews_given.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.requested_by.label: People who asked for his review
f.requested_by.formula: distinct humans who requested his review (fetched review requests only)
f.requested_by.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.teams_covered.label: Teams whose PRs he approved
f.teams_covered.formula: distinct teams (official team map) of the authors he approved
f.teams_covered.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.built_on_by.label: Later authors of the same files
f.built_on_by.formula: distinct authors who later changed, by ≥20 lines, a source file he had changed (shared hub files excluded)
f.built_on_by.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.changelog.label: PRs in the public changelog
f.changelog.formula: his window PRs cited in PostHog's public changelog
f.changelog.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl

f.issues_closed.label: Issues closed by his PRs
f.issues_closed.formula: distinct GitHub issues his merged PRs closed
f.issues_closed.source: recall.json metrics / coarse.json tier_counts / team_graph people / data/prs.jsonl
